metadata.title: Norfolk & Western R. Co. v. Ayers, 538 U.S. 135 (2003) (No. 01-963)
metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: Norfolk & Western R. Co. v. Ayers

Opinion filed: 2003-03-10

Docket No.: 01-963

Citations:
• 155 L. Ed. 2d 261
• 123 S. Ct. 1210
• 538 U.S. 135
• 2003 U.S. LEXIS 1956

Case holding summaries:
• "FELA renders common carrier railroads liable in damages to any person suffering injury while ... employed by [the] carrier if the injury or death result[ed] in whole or in part from the [carrier's] negligence."
• fear of bladder cancer from "benzidine test" on prisoner to detect blood on skin
• "It would be particularly curious for Congress to refer expressly to the established principle of comparative negligence, yet say not a word about adopting a new rule limiting the liability of the [defendant] on the basis of [another party's] negligence."
• joint and several liability remains the rule in admiralty
• "State laws are not controlling in determining what the incidents of this federal right shall be"
• plaintiff asserting noncancer asbestos claims may not recover any cancer-related damages
• sustaining jury charge allowing fear of cancer damages for plaintiff with "confirmed asbestosis"
• "The cost of human injury, an inescapable expense of railroading, must be borne by someone, and the FELA seeks to adjust that expense equitably between the worker and the carrier."
• predecessor statute declared unconstitutional because it regulated employee injuries not sufficiently related to interstate commerce
• sustaining a verdict including fear-of-cancer damages where trial judge found plaintiff "ha[d] a genuine, real believable fear of cancer" (internal quotation marks omitted)
• FELA decision holding erroneous "Trial Court's exclusion of evidence about [asbestosis claimant's] fear of cancer"
• occupational diseases caused by exposure to hazardous dusts are injuries under the FELA
• claim for fear of future disease held "clearly cognizable where, as here, plaintiff's exposure to asbestos has resulted in physical injury"
• fear of deterioration of hip bone following motor vehicle accident
• fear of cancer from ingestion of contaminated well water
• fear of cancer compensable, but plaintiff established cancer more likely than not to occur
• fear that brain injury from motor vehicle accident would lead to epilepsy
• fear of a recurrence of cancer when first cancer was untimely diagnosed as a result of medical malpractice
• railroad sued by employee under the FELA filed a third-party complaint against another party
• fear of illness from drinking contaminated well water
• toxic chemical spilled on hand
• denying fear-of-cancer damages to asbestosis claimant based in part on misplaced reliance on Metro-North Commuter R. Co. v. Buckley, 521 U. S. 424 (1997)
• sustaining award of damages that included compensation for asbestosis claimant's fear of cancer
• asbestosis claimants, who suffered "substantial bodily harm" from asbestos, may recover for fear of cancer
• apprehension of blood poisoning from foot injury
• "general concern for [one's] future health" held insufficient to support recovery for an asbestosis sufferer's fear of cancer
• sustaining jury charge allowing damages for asbestosis claimants' fear of cancer
• "[T]he inquiry in these cases today rarely presents more than the single question whether negligence of the employer played any part, however small, in the injury or death which is the subject of the suit."
• recovery permissible under the FELA only on showing that plaintiff will probably develop cancer from asbestos exposure
• "Where both the physical injury and the nervous shock are proximately caused by the same act of negligence, there is no necessity that the shock result exclusively from the physical injury."
• "Thus, damages for mental anguish concerning the chance that a future disease or condition will result from an original injury are generally not recoverable where the connection between the anxiety and the existing injury is too remote or tenuous"
• noting that Gottshall relied upon cases involving "a threatened physical contact that caused, or might have caused, immediate traumatic harm"
• denying fear-of-cancer recovery where condition "causes emotional distress only because the worker learns that he may become ill after a substantial period of time"
• "The common law permits emotional distress recovery for that category of plaintiffs who suffer from a disease."
• "emotional distress damages sought by asbestosis-afflicted plaintiff" found to fit "within a category where the law already permitted recovery for mental distress"
• "[C]ourts ... must consider the general impact ... of the general liability rules they ... create."
• describing joint and several liability as "settled by innumerable authorities" and citing federal decisions from 1883, 1893, 1894, 1895, 1902, 1904, 1906, 1910, and 1913
• evidence of increased risk of cancer held "admissible to establish, as a damage factor, the reasonableness of [an asbestosis claimant's] fear that he would contract cancer"
• "Once Congress has relied upon conditions that the courts have created, we are not as free as we would otherwise be to change them."
• prejudgment interest is not available under the FELA because it was unavailable at common law when the statute was enacted
• describing FELA's "central focus on physical perils"
• defining negligently inflicted emotional distress as "mental or emotional harm (such as fright or anxiety) that is caused by the negligence of another and that is not directly brought about by a physical injury"
• "[T]hese terms traditionally have been used to describe sensations stemming directly from a physical injury or condition" (internal quotation marks omitted)
• cancer evidence held admissible to show reasonableness of asbestosis claimant's fear of cancer
• “[I]t accords with the FELA’s overarching purpose to require the employer to bear the burden of identifying other responsible parties and demonstrating that some of the costs of the injury should be spread to them.”
• "those who escaped instant physical harm, but were `within the zone of danger of physical impact'"
• recovery allowed under "zone of danger" test for NIED where the plaintiff has been diagnosed with asbestosis, and damages for "fear of cancer" are alleged as part of the pain and suffering associated with existing asbestos-related disease
• "Many courts in recent years have considered the question presented here whether an asbestosis claimant may be compensated for fear of cancer. Of decisions that address the issue, a clear majority sustain recovery." [citing Cox ]
• "parasitic" generally defined as "associated with"
